video_title: Dan Ives: How to Survive AI’s Volatile "Air Pockets"
gist: Recorded the Monday before the midterms after a ~3.5% Nasdaq / ~6.5% SOX drop, Dan Nathan presses Dan Ives (now at Yorkville Ives) on AI 'air pockets': Ives argues this is year three of an 8-12 year buildout and favors buying thesis-intact dips (Microsoft/Azure, Alphabet, ServiceNow, cybersecurity), is cautious on debt-funded Oracle, and expects capex and monetization to flip around 2027, while Nathan counters with ~$800B of AI equity and debt raises, OpenAI's down-sized round, a shaky Anthropic IPO setup, GPU depreciation concerns, China open-source competition, and midterm/data-center moratorium risk.

themes.theme: AI cycle positioning and air pockets

insights.claim: Dan Ives views the current AI market as year three of an 8-to-10, possibly 12-year buildout, unlike the dot-com bubble, because it is funded by Big Tech with trillion-dollar balance sheets and $300-400 billion of annual free cash flow at around 20x earnings versus an average tech company at 32x revenues in March 2000.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Ives frames corrections as buyable air pockets rather than a bubble top.
insights.quote: If you go back to March 2000, the average tech company was 32 times revenues.

insights.claim: Ives estimates only about 3.5% of enterprises are down the AI path, with cybersecurity software AI penetration below 1%, which he sees as bullish runway.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Low penetration underpins a multi-year enterprise adoption thesis.

insights.claim: Hedge funds cannot simply take a 3-5 year view through capex-to-monetization air pockets because they could lose their jobs if positioned wrong, which amplifies volatility in names like ServiceNow and Alphabet.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Career-risk-driven institutional selling creates dislocations long-term holders can exploit.

insights.claim: Ives expects three or four times a year where certain AI-related stocks disconnect from fundamentals, and advises owning a core 20-30 stock list and buying thesis-intact names on sharp selloffs rather than trading 60-90 day theses.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Volatility is a recurring entry mechanism rather than a signal of thesis failure.

insights.claim: Stock picking has become critical because two names in the same AI category can be drastically differently positioned.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Dispersion within AI favors selective rather than basket exposure.
insights.quote: Two names could be drastically different position and if they are like you have to own the one that's right.

insights.claim: Ives sees 2027 as the low-water mark when capex and monetization flip, and expects a tech bull market over the next three years if the transition is managed well.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A dated inflection point for when AI ROI should become visible.

insights.claim: The prior Friday the Nasdaq fell about 3.5% and the SOX about 6.5%, with Mag 7 names hit following weakness at Meta and Google; Dan Nathan notes he can't recall a calendar Q3 reporter whose stock traded well afterward.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Earnings season has been punishing even for good prints, signalling positioning exhaustion.

insights.claim: Ives believes street estimates underestimate Microsoft Azure growth by 15-20% over the next 18-24 months as enterprises move to AI, supporting a sum-of-the-parts value of $650-700 per share.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Microsoft is Ives' highest-conviction table-pounder, especially after its 35% drawdown to ~$360.

insights.claim: Azure growth and Office 365 Copilot adoption are tightly interconnected, and for core Microsoft enterprise customers the path of least resistance is to stay with Microsoft, which has smoothed earlier Copilot frustration.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Enterprise lock-in protects Microsoft's AI share even as GCP and AWS accelerate.

insights.claim: Dan Nathan cites GCP growing 100% year-over-year last quarter and AWS reaccelerating from a low-teens bottom to 39% growth.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: All three hyperscalers are seeing strong cloud demand, raising the bar for share gains.

insights.claim: Ives estimates the market is pricing a 30-40% discount on Alphabet's future advertising business due to AI cannibalization fears, and argues that any outcome better than this worst case gives the stock significant upside.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Alphabet's ad-cannibalization fear may be over-discounted.
insights.quote: investors are probably putting a 30 to 40% discount on the future advertising business of Google

insights.claim: Ives expects Alphabet's search weakness to be viewed in coming quarters as an air pocket rather than a secular decline, as CMOs he speaks with expect Google to find an AI-era monetization engine as Microsoft did with Copilot.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Monetization of AI search is a race against the clock for Google.

insights.claim: Anthropic has said it will not put advertising on Claude, while OpenAI has started an advertising business, which feeds a concern that chatbots could undermine the digital ad model that subsidizes much of the internet economy.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Ad-funded business models broadly, not just Google, face disruption risk.

insights.claim: Ives has been cautious to negative on Oracle, which is rare for him, because of the heavy debt it is taking on to build itself into a hyperscaler largely for one customer, with about $300 billion of its $600 billion tied to OpenAI.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Debt-funded AI buildouts are being differentiated from cash-flow-funded ones.

insights.claim: Credit markets are differentiating debt-dependent AI builders from cash-flow-funded ones, with Oracle and CoreWeave CDS being the poster children that unsettle investors; Nathan sees Oracle as the obvious canary in the coal mine in any sustained selloff.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Watch Oracle and CoreWeave credit spreads as an early warning for the AI trade.

insights.claim: Ives names three biggest risks to the AI revolution: political risk around the midterms such as a blue wave slowing buildouts, energy shortages for deploying GPUs, and the gap between capex and monetization, which until shortened will cause credit spreads to blow out.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A concise risk checklist for the AI bull thesis.

themes.theme: Capital raising glut and AI IPOs

insights.claim: Dan Nathan tallies this year's AI-related raises: equity including OpenAI $122 billion, Anthropic $95 billion, SpaceX $75 billion IPO, Alphabet $85 billion, Oracle $25 billion and xAI $20 billion; debt including Amazon $54 billion, Alphabet about $30 billion, Oracle $25 billion, Meta $25 billion and about $400 billion of bond issuance overall, totaling a little over $800 billion.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Massive supply of AI paper raises the question of who absorbs it and at what price.

insights.claim: OpenAI reportedly tried to raise $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation but after over a month was only able to raise $20 billion at $1.2 trillion, which Nathan sees as cooling demand that bodes poorly for Anthropic's IPO.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: A down-sized, lower-valuation round suggests private-market appetite for frontier labs is peaking.

insights.claim: Ives would be shocked if Anthropic's IPO, targeted at roughly $1.5 trillion, does not happen given strong private-market price discovery, while Nathan would be surprised if it can be done in this environment and warns poor sequential Q3 numbers in an updated S-1 could be a disaster for markets.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives / Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: The Anthropic IPO is a key sentiment event for the AI trade.

insights.claim: Nathan notes Anthropic's revenue growth is decelerating and that its plan to build its own data centers puts it in competition with compute suppliers like xAI and Oracle whose contracts with it are not long-term.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Vertical integration by labs could destabilize neocloud and Oracle demand.

insights.claim: SpaceX traded up to about 20% over its IPO price and higher for a week but is now back at its IPO price roughly three and a half months later.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Mega-IPO buyers chasing early pops have not been rewarded.

insights.claim: To own these AI stocks Ives says you must believe demand produces free cash flow in 2028-2030 and that the ability to raise capital puts a floor under the leaders, since those without funds cannot be tier-one in the AI arms race.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Access to capital itself is treated as a competitive moat.

insights.claim: Ives launched IVAI, the Ives Ultra fund, via a $200 million IPO as a public vehicle investing in private AI tech companies, and Yorkville Ives has hired about 25 people while he remains associated with the Wedbush Ives ETF.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Retail access to private AI via listed vehicles is expanding.

themes.theme: Neoclouds, GPU depreciation and token economics

insights.claim: Jim Chanos's bear argument is that Nvidia books GPU profits upfront while buyers like Microsoft depreciate them over about six years, a double benefit to S&P 500 earnings, and that many purchased GPUs sit undeployed due to energy, data-center and memory bottlenecks.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Accounting timing may flatter AI earnings; Ives concedes rubber meets the road in 6-9 months.

insights.claim: Elon Musk has suggested only seven to ten neoclouds may survive, and Nathan argues a shakeout would create a compute glut weighing on hyperscaler valuations even if it helps them long term; Ives expects consolidation among players like CoreWeave and Nebius.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan / Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Neocloud consolidation is a musical-chairs risk for leveraged compute providers.

insights.claim: SpaceX is building itself into a hyperscaler/neocloud and has struck large compute deals with Anthropic and Google, making it partly a competitor to neoclouds.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives / Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Musk's commentary on neoclouds is not neutral.

insights.claim: Musk signaled the end of 'token maxing' for Grok, saying unlimited usage was unsustainable and moving to a pricing model, a shift Meta may also face with Muse.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Consumer AI is moving from subsidized usage to consumption pricing.

insights.claim: Ives expects token prices to keep falling and models to become more commoditized, though the consequences will not fully hit for a few years.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Model commoditization pressures pure-play labs like OpenAI and Anthropic most.

themes.theme: Software, cybersecurity and IT spending disruption

insights.claim: Ives views the 'SaaS apocalypse' selloff as baby-with-the-bathwater and a generational near-term opportunity, citing ServiceNow's customer base, partners and leadership under McDermott as reasons to own it on violent drawdowns.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Ives is buying beaten-down software names where the thesis is intact.

insights.claim: Nathan argues Salesforce's stock was saved on a recent quarter by Dario appearing alongside Benioff, calling such commercial partnerships routine 'funny business' as frontier labs need enterprise deals.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Lab partnership announcements may be overvalued as signals of SaaS resilience.

insights.claim: Ives expects cybersecurity budgets could double over the next two to three years as agents expand the attack surface, and sees hacks as increasing demand for CrowdStrike, Palo Alto and Zscaler rather than undermining sentiment.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: AI-driven hacking acceleration is a tailwind for leading security platforms.

insights.claim: Fortinet fell about 25% after a soft quarter, which Ives distinguishes from CrowdStrike and Palo Alto because Fortinet sits more on the firewall side.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives / Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Hardware-centric security is diverging from cloud/AI-native security.

insights.claim: Ives says IT spending disruption is unlike anything in his ~30 years covering software: deals expected to convert from pipelines are being pulled because they are not AI-related or because budgets shift to AI projects, leaving some CEOs seemingly lost.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Pipeline conversion rates for non-AI software are deteriorating, a key earnings risk.
insights.quote: the level of disruption that's happening across the IT spending cycle is unlike anything we've ever seen

insights.claim: Intel fell about 30% on a gut-punch quarter despite memory and PC CPU dynamics being well known; the US government had invested at $20 and Nvidia at $25 in summer 2025, after which the stock ran hundreds of percent.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan / Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Even well-telegraphed cycle names can see violent drawdowns after big runs.

insights.claim: Reddit fell 30% on Friday as AI models take its data, pushing it toward a closed web, and agentic AI has also hit travel companies.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Open-web content and intermediary businesses are being disrupted by AI agents.

insights.claim: A Goldman Sachs report cited by Nathan says 77% of global token usage comes from China while China accounts for only 22% of spend, driven by cheap open-source models that he fears China will push globally like a digital Belt and Road.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Cheap Chinese open-source models threaten the pricing power behind US lab valuations.
insights.quote: 77% of the global token usage is coming from China

insights.claim: Ives argues the US is for the first time in 30 years well ahead of China in tech thanks to Nvidia and frontier models, though China leads in physical AI, robotics and energy with a more receptive regulatory environment.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: US tech leadership is the core of the AI bull case, while robotics is China's edge.

insights.claim: Ives says Alibaba executives prefer domestic chips over Nvidia, which is why Jensen believes Nvidia must sell into China, and notes Nvidia trades at 11-12x earnings, perhaps 9x on real numbers.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Nvidia's valuation looks low despite custom silicon competition.

insights.claim: Nathan notes Nvidia faces more competition than ever from custom silicon, including Anthropic deals in which Blackstone, Apollo and Broadcom backstop its purchases of Google TPUs.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: TPU and custom ASIC adoption is eroding Nvidia's inference share.

insights.claim: Ives's biggest worry is politicization of data-center buildouts, such as moratoriums after a midterm blue wave, while Nathan notes Texas Governor Abbott has imposed a moratorium on new data centers; Ives argues data centers and jobs will simply relocate between states.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives / Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: State-level data center policy is an emerging risk to AI capex timelines.

insights.claim: Nathan cites Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson seeing the midterms and AI capex trepidation as a possible clearing event with an S&P 500 target of 8,000 that requires hyperscaler participation.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Sell-side bulls still see major index upside contingent on big tech.
